summary: Describes how PGP can be used to provide privacy and authentication for email using the MIME security content types. It lets mail programs encrypt and sign messages in a standard MIME structure.

eli5.summary: It is a way to put a secret and signed letter into an email in a form that every mail program can understand.

questions: how to use pgp with mime
how to encrypt email with pgp
subtitle: How to wrap PGP-encrypted and PGP-signed data inside standard MIME email messages.

tldr.problem: Earlier ways of mixing PGP with MIME email, including the withdrawn application/pgp content type, made it impossible to recover a signed message body without parsing PGP-specific data structures.
tldr.mechanism: It uses the multipart/signed and multipart/encrypted formats from RFC 1847 and defines three content types: application/pgp-encrypted, application/pgp-signature and application/pgp-keys. The signed text and the signature travel in separate body parts.
tldr.outcome: Mail programs get a standard way to carry PGP privacy and authentication. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has since been updated by RFC 3156.

facts.label: Parts in encrypted or signed multipart

today: RFC 2015 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 3156, so read that RFC alongside it. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why PGP Needed a MIME Format
sections.content:
Earlier attempts to combine PGP (Pretty Good Privacy) with MIME email, including the since withdrawn application/pgp content type, had a serious flaw. A reader could not recover a signed message body without parsing data structures that are specific to PGP.

This RFC instead builds on the security multipart formats of RFC 1847. Those formats clearly separate the signed message body from the signature. The document is styled after RFC 1848, which defines MIME Object Security Services (MOSS).

It defines three new content types: application/pgp-encrypted, application/pgp-signature and application/pgp-keys. An implementation is compliant only if it obeys every item labeled MUST or REQUIRED.
sections.eli5: People had tried to mix secret-letter software with email before, but the signed message got tangled up with the signature. This RFC keeps the letter and the signature in separate envelopes.

sections.title: PGP Output Formats and Transfer Encoding Limits
sections.content:
PGP can produce either ASCII armor or 8-bit binary output. ASCII armor is the REQUIRED method for data transfer, so people whose software cannot interpret these formats can still extract the PGP data from the message. If the data is too large for one message, the MIME message/partial mechanism should be used rather than the multipart ASCII armor PGP format.

Mail gateways may convert a message to Quoted-Printable or Base64 when the next hop lacks MIME or 8-bit support. That would break a signature. For this reason all data signed under this protocol MUST be constrained to 7 bits, with 8-bit data encoded as Quoted-Printable or Base64. The rule also applies when signed data is then encrypted. Data that is only encrypted may contain 8-bit characters.

The implementor's note advises being conservative in what you generate and liberal in what you accept: accept any content-transfer-encoding, but generate only the 7-bit format.
sections.eli5: Some mail systems rewrite letters that look unusual, and that would ruin a signature, like a seal that breaks when someone repackages the letter. So signed letters must use only plain, simple characters.

sections.title: PGP Encrypted Data
sections.content:
Before encryption, the data should be written in MIME canonical format, covering both body and headers. The result is carried in a multipart/encrypted message whose protocol parameter MUST be "application/pgp-encrypted", enclosed in quotes.

The multipart MUST have exactly two parts. The first has content type application/pgp-encrypted and holds the control information. A compliant message MUST contain Version: 1 there, because the PGP packet format already carries everything else needed for decryption. The second part holds the encrypted data and is labeled application/octet-stream.
sections.eli5: An encrypted email has two envelopes. The small one says which version of the lock was used, and the big one holds the locked letter.

sections.title: PGP Signed Data
sections.content:
Signed messages use multipart/signed with a protocol parameter that MUST be "application/pgp-signature" (quoted). The micalg parameter MUST be pgp-<hash-symbol>, naming the message integrity check used. The defined hash symbols are md5 and sha1.

There are exactly two parts. The first holds the signed data in MIME canonical format with its content headers. The second holds the PGP signature, labeled application/pgp-signature. To sign, the sender converts the data to canonical form (for text/plain, line endings become CR LF), applies a Content-Transfer-Encoding, and adds MIME content headers. The signature MUST cover both the data and its headers, and MUST be generated detached so the signed data is not altered.

On receipt, an application MUST convert line endings to the canonical CR LF form, because the local MTA may have changed them. It then passes the signed data, its content headers and the signature to the verification service. The RFC also suggests Quoted-Printable encoding when a line begins with From , encoding the F, so that a mail transport agent does not insert a > and invalidate the signature.
sections.eli5: A signed email is a letter plus a separate stamp that proves who wrote it. The stamp covers the letter exactly as written, so if anyone changes even a comma, the stamp no longer matches.

sections.title: Signing and Encrypting Together
sections.content:
The RFC allows two ways to both sign and encrypt. The first follows RFC 1847: sign the data as multipart/signed, then encrypt that whole body to form the final multipart/encrypted object.

The second is a combined method. Versions 2.x of PGP can sign and encrypt in one operation, which the RFC calls an acceptable shortcut with less overhead. The result is formed as a multipart/encrypted object and MUST follow the same canonicalization rules as multipart/signed. An agent is explicitly allowed to decrypt a combined message and rewrite it as multipart/signed, using the signature data embedded in the encrypted version.
sections.eli5: You can first sign a letter and then lock it in a box, or use a gadget that does both in one step. Both work, and the receiver can open the box and keep the signed letter.

sections.title: Distributing Public Keys
sections.content: The application/pgp-keys content type is the one to use for relaying public key blocks. It has no required parameters and no optional parameters. The RFC says nothing more about how keys are obtained or trusted.
sections.eli5: If you want friends to send you locked letters, you mail them your public padlock. This content type is the label on that package.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC's security section is brief. Using this protocol has the same security considerations as PGP itself, and it is not known to either increase or decrease the security of messages that use it. The reader is pointed to RFC 1991, "PGP Message Exchange Formats", for details.
sections.eli5: Putting PGP in an email wrapper does not make it stronger or weaker. It is as safe as PGP already was.
